newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian engineering unions threaten to strike.
newsitem.headline: Italian engineering unions threaten to strike.

text.p: Trades unions representing Italy's engineering and metalworkers are threatening an industry-wide strike in a push for higher pay just as the centre-left government begins to tackle a key 1997 budget package.

In July, talks setting wage levels for around 1.5 million engineering workers for 1997 and 1998 broke down, and next Monday a special meeting of three main engineering unions, Fiom, Fim and Uilm, may call a strike by the end of September.

"I think the decision will be for a stoppage because Federmeccanica (the association of engineering and metal employers) has not changed its stance in respect of July," said Luigi Angeletti, leader of the Uilm union.

Tino Magni, leader of the Fiom union in Italy's northern industrial heartland of Lombardy, echoed Angeletti's views. "We are still open to negotiate but margins are very narrow for a strike to be avoided," he said.
A general metal workers strike to support contract renewal would be the first in the last six years.

Michele Figurati, general director of Federmeccanica, used a smoother tone. "I wouldn't dramatise the announcement of the trade unions...in July we didn't break up, we just postponed the negotiations," he told Reuters.

The engineering and metalworkers, whose contracts expired in June, have demanded an overall wage rise of 10.1 percent for the next two years. This includes a loss of purchasing power of 4.1 percent for June 1994-June 1996, plus six percent to cover forecast inflation (three percent both for 1996 and 1997).

"We offered a range of increase between seven and nine percent, in line with other contracts already renewed...We need a global valutation that must be consistent with the situation of the industries already burdened by heavy labour cost," Figurati said.
Asked if talks could start again even if a strike was called, Figurati answered, "Negotiation can always be resumed."
Italy's Treasury minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi is eagerly looking for a decrease in inflation to obtain an easing in the interest rate that Italy has to pay on his huge budget deficit.

Italy's preliminary consumer price inflation showed a fall in August to 3.3-3.4 percent year-on-year after a 3.6 percent rise in July and 5.8 percent a year ago. Ciampi's inflation target for the next year is 2.5 percent.

Sergio Cofferati, leader of the biggest italian trade union, Cgil, said on Monday in an interview to the daily L'Unita that the government must continue to fight inflation, "but acting on tariffs and prices and not on the consumer front".
"We must encourage consumers to regaing purchasing power and this is the contract's main task," Cofferati added.
The hard-left Communist Refoundation party, whose 35 seats are needed by the government to have a majority in the lower house, said workers' purchasing power has been eroded too much.
Refoundation votes will be crucial to pass the government's 32.4 trillion deficit-cutting 1997 budget.

It is aimed at cutting Italy's budget deficit to gross domestic product ratio to 4.5 percent in 1997 from the current six percent in an effort to stick as close as possible to the three percent criteria required to joint a European single currency in 1999.
